In order to study the phenomenon that the elongation is greatly increased at 900 °C, we analyze the microstructure and crystal microdomain orientation of the sample after tensile test at 900 °C.

A powder metallurgy Ti-48Al alloy with a diameter of 100 mm and a height of 500 mm was manufactured via vacuum sintering at 1250 °C for 120 min, and the relative density of as-sintered alloy is about 97%.
A cylindrical blank with dimensions of Φ100 × 400 mm 3 was cut from the as-sintered alloy, and then vacuum canned into 304 stainless steel.

In order to achieve a high forging rate (1 × 10−1 s−1), the canned billet was forged at 1300 °C higher than the sintering temperature. The billet was forged by a two-step forging process with a deformation of 50 % in each step.
The forged billet was annealed at 1250 °C for 30 min after first forging, while the billet was air-cooled to room temperature after the second forging.

The alloy consists of α2-Ti3Al phase and γ-TiAl phase, and has a near-γ microstructure with equiaxed grains. The average grain size is about 10 µm. As shown in Fig. 1(b), the bright area is α2-Ti3Al phase, while the grey area is γ phase. In addition, the relative density of as-sintered alloy is about 97%, so there are some unclosed pores in the alloy. Besides, the volume fraction of γ phase of as-sintered alloy is 86.3%, while the volume fraction of α2 phase is 13.7%.

Different from the stress-strain curve at room temperature, the curve at 900 °C exhibits an obvious characteristic of DRX. In the initial stage of deformation, the stress increases rapidly with the increase of strain, and the maximum stress value can be reached when the strain is small. After reaching the maximum stress, the flow stress decreases significantly with increasing strain. Due to the softening effect of DRX, the elongation is greatly increased.
